cdn.guideSubtitle: Create a scoped API token, copy the Zone ID, then let Ploydok create the proxied DNS record and cache rule.
cdn.step1Copy: In Cloudflare, open My Profile, then API Tokens. Use a custom token so permissions stay scoped to one zone.
cdn.step1Alt: Cloudflare profile page with API Tokens selected
cdn.step1Caption: Profile sidebar: open API Tokens before creating the custom token.
cdn.step2Copy: Choose Custom token. Avoid the global API key: Ploydok only needs DNS, cache rules, and purge permissions.
cdn.step2Alt: Cloudflare custom API token permission form
cdn.step2Caption: Cloudflare custom token screen: token name, permissions, and zone resources.
cdn.step3Copy: Cloudflare permission names can vary by account, but this is the target shape for DNS + Cache Rules + purge.
cdn.step3Caption: Permissions area: add one row for each Cloudflare permission Ploydok needs.
cdn.step4Copy: Before creation, verify that the permissions and zone resources are scoped to the domain that owns your app hostname.
cdn.step4Alt: Cloudflare API token summary before creation
cdn.step4Caption: Cloudflare summary screen: confirm the scoped token before creating it.
cdn.step5Copy: Paste the token once in Ploydok. For Zone ID, open the zone Overview page in Cloudflare and copy the Zone ID from the API panel.
cdn.step5Caption: Cloudflare only shows the generated token once. Copy it before closing this screen.
cdn.step6Copy: Hostname is the public app domain. Origin is where Cloudflare should point the proxied DNS record: your Ploydok origin hostname or server IP.

storage.title: Storage
storage.description: Persistent app volumes and their local or S3-compatible backups.
storage.createDesc: Volumes are mounted into the app container and retained across redeploys. Deleting a volume requires the app to be stopped.
storage.name: Name
storage.step1Body: Choose a short name and an absolute mount path. The path is where your app reads and writes persistent files inside the container, for example /data, /uploads, or /var/www/html/storage.
storage.mountBody: The mount path is the folder inside the app container that becomes persistent. Use the folder your framework already writes user files to; files written elsewhere can disappear after a rebuild or redeploy.
storage.step2Body: A volume is attached when the runtime container is created. Existing containers keep their current mounts until the next restart or deploy.
storage.step3Body: Use Backup now for an immediate snapshot, or configure a policy. Local backups stay on this machine; S3-compatible backups can target R2, AWS S3, Scaleway, OVH, or another compatible endpoint.
storage.step4Body: Stop the app before deleting a volume. Ploydok keeps the delete action explicit because removing a volume can remove user-generated data.
storage.noteDb: Keep database data in managed databases, not app volumes.
storage.noteOne: Prefer one volume per concern, such as uploads, cache, or application storage.
storage.noteRestore: Test restore procedures before relying on a backup policy in production.

advanced.title: Caddy Extra Handlers
advanced.description: Add custom Caddy handlers (headers, rewrite, redir, static_response, request_body, vars) to your app route. Learn more in the {{docs}}.
advanced.howItWorksBody: the JSON below is merged into the Caddy route handler chain for this app, in front of the reverse proxy. The Caddy Admin API rejects invalid JSON server-side — your previous handler chain stays in place if validation fails, so a bad paste never takes the app offline. Save again with a corrected config to re-apply.
